tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

# wordstat: Interface Contract

## Constraints

- **Stack:** Python >=3.11, standard library only; pytest for tests only.
- **Package location:** `wordstat/` at repo root (flat layout, no `src/`).
- **Entry point:** `python -m wordstat ...` run from repo root.

## Functional requirements

- **R1** `python -m wordstat --help` exits 0.
- **R2** `python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE` reads exactly one file, decoded as UTF-8 with an optional BOM (`utf-8-sig`). stdin is never read.
- **R3** Counts, computed on the decoded text:
  - `lines` = `len(text.splitlines())`
  - `words` = number of matches of `[a-z0-9]+` in `text.lower()`
  - `chars` = `len(text)` (code points, BOM excluded)
- **R4** `top` lists the `N` most frequent words (same tokens as R3), ordered by count descending, then word ascending. `--top` defaults to 3. Fewer than `N` distinct words lists all of them.
- **R5** Default output is the text format; `--json` selects the JSON format.
- **R6** Output is deterministic: UTF-8, `\n` line endings, no locale use. stdout is reconfigured to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`.

## Interface contract

### Command

```
python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE
```

- argparse `prog` is `wordstat`.
- `--top` must be an integer >= 1, else usage error.

### Text format

Exactly four lines, each ending in `\n`:

```
lines: <lines>
words: <words>
chars: <chars>
top: <word>=<count> <word>=<count> ...
```

With no words, the last line is `top:` with no trailing space.

### JSON format

One line: the result of `json.dumps(obj)` with default separators, followed by `\n`, where `obj` has keys in this order:

```
{"lines": <int>, "words": <int>, "chars": <int>, "top": [{"word": <str>, "count": <int>}, ...]}
```

### Exit codes and errors

Errors print one line to stderr, prefix `wordstat: error: `, and leave stdout empty. `<path>` is the FILE argument exactly as given.

| Condition | Exit | stderr (after prefix) |
|---|---|---|
| File missing, a directory, or unreadable | 3 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
| Not valid UTF-8 | 3 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |
| Usage error (missing FILE, unknown flag, bad `--top`) | 2 | argparse default; the last stderr line must match `^wordstat: error: ` |

Exit 0 on success, including an empty file. Exit 1 is reserved for unexpected internal errors.

## Example

`sample.txt` (UTF-8, `\n` endings):

```
The cat sat.
The cat ran!
A dog.
```

`python -m wordstat sample.txt` → exit 0, stdout:

```
lines: 3
words: 8
chars: 33
top: cat=2 the=2 a=1
```

`python -m wordstat --json --top 2 sample.txt` → exit 0, stdout:

```
{"lines": 3, "words": 8, "chars": 33, "top": [{"word": "cat", "count": 2}, {"word": "the", "count": 2}]}
```

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

# Spec Research & Authoring

Deploy a parallel research team to investigate requirements for a new spec, then synthesize findings into a complete feature specification document. The research phase uses 3 subagents with distinct investigation angles to ensure comprehensive coverage before writing begins.

## Arguments

Accept a spec topic or folder path (e.g., `notifications`, `feature-007`, `docs/notifications/`, or a plain description like "real-time notifications system").  
If a stub README already exists in the feature folder (for example `docs/feature-name/README.md`), read it for initial scope constraints.

## Workflow

### Phase 1: Scope Discovery

Before dispatching researchers:

1. Determine the feature folder name. If the argument is already a folder path, use it. Otherwise derive `docs/spec-NNN-<kebab-slug>/`: read `CLAUDE.md` `## Current State` for the current sequence if present. If `CLAUDE.md` is missing, malformed, or the `## Current State` section is absent, continue with fallback naming logic: list existing `docs/spec-*` folders and use the highest number + 1. If no numbered folders exist, follow whatever folder convention prior specs in `docs/` use; if `docs/` is empty, ask the user to confirm the folder name before proceeding.
2. Read any existing stub (`docs/<folder>/README.md`) for scope constraints.
3. Scan the codebase for existing patterns and integration points.
4. Identify 3 distinct research angles based on what the feature needs to cover.

### Phase 2: Define 3 Research Angles

Select 3 non-overlapping research angles based on the feature domain. Each agent investigates a different facet.

Typical per-domain configurations (infrastructure / domain-feature / security-compliance, always anchored by a Codebase Analyst) are in `references/research-angle-menus.md` — load it when picking the angles.

### Phase 3: Dispatch Research Team in Parallel

Deploy all 3 researchers simultaneously.

- **Codebase Analyst**: use `geeky-orchestration:code-explorer` agent type.
- **Web Researchers (2)**: use `general-purpose` agent type with instructions to use `WebSearch` and `WebFetch`.

Each research brief ends with:

```
Produce a structured report with:
- Key findings (numbered, specific)
- Constraints discovered (what the spec MUST respect)
- Recommendations (what the spec SHOULD include)
- Sources (URLs for web research, file paths for codebase)

DO NOT create or modify any files.
```

### Phase 4: Synthesize into Spec Document

After all 3 researchers report back:

1. Consolidate findings: merge overlap, resolve contradictions, and note confidence gaps.
2. Define scope: goals, non-goals, delegation items.
3. Write the requirements document using the project’s established conventions in:
   - `docs/<feature-folder>/feature-specification.md`
   - `docs/<feature-folder>/README.md`

   Do not create `SPEC-NNNN-*.md` files — that naming is legacy; `feature-specification.md` is the canonical filename consumed by /geeky-plan and the freeze hooks.

   If a stub README already exists, preserve its stated scope and only update the Status line and missing sections; otherwise create the README stub:

   ```markdown
   # [Feature Name]

   [One-paragraph scope summary.]

   **Status:** Spec written — not yet planned
   **Spec:** `feature-specification.md`
   **Next:** /geeky-plan docs/<feature-folder>/
   ```

Use the 11-section recommended spec structure in `references/spec-structure-template.md` (adapt sections to the feature domain; include citations and explicit assumptions at the end of major findings).

### Phase 5: Commit and Suggest Next Steps

Commit the spec (same command on all platforms). The spec is not yet frozen — it only becomes part of the frozen planning contract after /geeky-plan runs:

```
git add docs/<feature-folder>/
git commit -m "docs: author feature specification in <feature-folder>" -m "[1-line summary of the spec focus]" -m "Research conducted by: codebase analyst, researcher 2 domain, researcher 3 domain"
```

Then suggest next steps:
```
Spec written. Next steps:
- /geeky-plan docs/<feature-folder>/   (to create implementation plan, tasks, kanban)
- /plan-review docs/<feature-folder>/  (to validate the planning package)
- /geeky-implement docs/<feature-folder>/ (to execute)
```

## Research Quality Standards

- **Recency**: Target sources from roughly the past 18 months; avoid older sources unless they cover stable fundamentals.
- **Authority**: Prefer official documentation (Microsoft Learn, AWS docs, RFC specs) over blogs or forums.
- **Specificity**: Include concrete findings (resource types, API versions, package versions, pricing tiers).
- **Adversarial verification**: If researchers disagree on a fact, preserve both positions and flag for user decision.

## Rules

- **Always 3 researchers** — one codebase analyst + two web/domain researchers.
- **Parallel dispatch** — all 3 in a single turn for maximum speed.
- **Research before writing** — do not start the spec document until all researchers report back.
- **Cite sources** — every major claim in the spec should trace to research.
- **Respect existing stubs** — if a README stub exists, treat its stated scope as authoritative unless research justifies adjustments.
- **Follow project conventions** — spec format, naming, and folder structure should match prior specs in `docs/`.

# Deterministic cross-platform CLI I/O for `wordstat` — research report

## Numbered key findings

1. **`sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")` is the documented mechanism for pinned stdout bytes.** `TextIOWrapper.reconfigure(*, encoding=None, errors=None, newline=None, ...)` "Reconfigure this text stream using new settings for encoding, errors, newline, line_buffering and write_through." Unspecified parameters keep current settings, "except `errors='strict'` is used when *encoding* is specified but *errors* is not specified." Timing: "It is not possible to change the encoding or newline if some data has already been read from the stream. On the other hand, changing encoding after write is possible." "This method does an implicit stream flush before setting the new parameters." — https://docs.python.org/3/library/io.html#io.TextIOWrapper.reconfigure

2. **`newline="\n"` (or `''`) is what suppresses Windows `\r\n` translation on write.** For writing: "if *newline* is `None`, any `'\n'` characters written are translated to the system default line separator, `os.linesep`. If *newline* is `''` or `'\n'`, no translation takes place." Contract R6 pins `newline="\n"`, which is the no-translation setting. The default (`None`) would make identical code emit `\r\n` on Windows and break byte-for-byte determinism. Same semantics are documented for `open()`'s `newline` parameter. — https://docs.python.org/3/library/io.html#io.TextIOWrapper.newline and https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open

3. **stdout and stderr are ordinary text streams with locale/`PYTHONIOENCODING`-influenced encodings unless overridden.** "These streams are regular text files like those returned by the `open()` function." Their encoding "is initialized from `PyConfig.stdio_encoding` and `PyConfig.stdio_errors`"; "On Windows, UTF-8 is used for the console device. Non-character devices such as disk files and pipes use the system locale encoding." Also: "the `stderr` stream is line-buffered in both cases." So without `reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")`, redirected stdout on Windows can be ANSI-codepage-encoded — nondeterministic across machines. "Under some conditions `stdin`, `stdout` and `stderr` ... can be `None`" (pythonw / GUI), which matters if you ever call `reconfigure` unconditionally. — https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.stdin

4. **argparse usage errors already match the contract's exit-2 shape.** `ArgumentParser.error(message)` "prints a usage message, including the *message*, to `sys.stderr` and terminates the program with a status code of 2." Example shape: `usage: PROG [-h] ...` then `PROG: error: argument --foo: invalid int value: 'spam'`. With `prog='wordstat'`, the last stderr line is literally `wordstat: error: ...`, satisfying the contract's `^wordstat: error: ` requirement without any custom formatting. `exit_on_error` (3.9+) defaults to `True`, so `parse_args()` raises `SystemExit(2)` rather than `ArgumentError` — do not set it to `False`. — https://docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html

5. **argparse `prog` is not stable by default and must be set explicitly.** `prog` defaults to being "generated from the `__main__` module attributes and `sys.argv[0]`", and "Changed in version 3.14: The default `prog` value now reflects how `__main__` was actually executed". Running as `python -m wordstat` would otherwise yield a different prog string than `python -m wordstat` invoked under another interpreter path. Contract requires `prog` is `wordstat`. — https://docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html

6. **argparse help/usage on success go to stdout (needed for R1); error/exit messages go to stderr.** `print_usage(file=None)` / `print_help(file=None)`: "If *file* is `None`, `sys.stdout` is assumed." `exit(status=0, message=None)`: "if given, it prints a *message* to `sys.stderr`". `-h`/`--help` therefore exits 0 with help on stdout, while usage errors leave stdout empty — matching R1 and the error table. — https://docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html

7. **`utf-8-sig` is the documented codec for BOM-tolerant UTF-8 reads; do not use it for output.** "On decoding `utf-8-sig` will skip those three bytes if they appear as the first three bytes in the file." And critically for output: "On encoding the utf-8-sig codec will write `0xef`, `0xbb`, `0xbf` as the first three bytes to the file" — using it to write would prefix a BOM and break R6/R5 output. Plain `utf-8` treats a decoded `U+FEFF` as a regular character, which would inflate `chars`; contract R2 (`utf-8-sig`) and R3 ("BOM excluded") align with decoding only. — https://docs.python.org/3/library/codecs.html#standard-encodings and https://docs.python.org/3/howto/unicode.html

8. **Default decoding is not portable across 3.11–3.14, so the encoding must always be passed explicitly.** `open()`: "In text mode, if *encoding* is not specified, UTF-8 is used by default; if Python UTF-8 Mode is disabled, `locale.getencoding()` is called" — and "Changed in version 3.15: UTF-8 is now the default encoding, instead of the platform-dependent locale encoding (PEP 686)". On 3.11–3.13 in particular the implicit default is the locale encoding (e.g. `cp1252` on Western Windows). Explicit `encoding="utf-8-sig"` is what makes the read deterministic; the contract already mandates it. — https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open and https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.15.html

9. **Invalid UTF-8 surfaces as `UnicodeDecodeError`; unreadable paths surface as `OSError` subclasses.** `errors='strict'` (the default) "raise[s] a `UnicodeDecodeError` exception" on undecodable input — this is the signal to map to exit 3 / `<path>: not valid UTF-8`. `open()`: "If the file cannot be opened, an `OSError` is raised"; `FileNotFoundError` ("Raised when a file or directory is requested but doesn't exist") and `IsADirectoryError` ("Raised when a file operation is requested on a directory") are `OSError` subclasses — map all of these (plus permission errors) to exit 3 / `<path>: cannot read file`, per the contract table. — https://docs.python.org/3/howto/unicode.html, https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open

10. **`json.dumps` with default arguments is already deterministic given an ordered dict literal.** Default separators: "If `None` (the default), *separators* defaults to `(', ', ': ')` if *indent* is `None`" — contract's "default separators" means `', '` and `': '`, i.e. `{"lines": 3, ...}` with spaces, not compact form. `sort_keys` "Default `False`" — correct, since the contract fixes key order explicitly. Order is stable because "Dictionaries preserve insertion order" and "Changed in version 3.7: Dictionary order is guaranteed to be insertion order" — so building the object with keys `lines, words, chars, top` in that literal order yields the contracted order on every run/platform. — https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json.dumps and https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#mapping-types-dict

11. **`ensure_ascii=True` (the default) further stabilizes output bytes.** "If *True* (the default), the output is guaranteed to have all incoming non-ASCII and non-printable characters escaped." Words are matched as `[a-z0-9]+` so tokens are pure ASCII anyway, but keeping the default means any non-ASCII that ever reaches the object is escaped to `\uXXXX`, so the output line is pure ASCII and independent of the terminal/pipe encoding. — https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json.dumps

12. **Unicode token matching caveat for the counting regex.** "In Python 3, Unicode characters are matched by default for `str` patterns." The caution in the docs is specific to `IGNORECASE`: "when the Unicode patterns `[a-z]` or `[A-Z]` are used in combination with the IGNORECASE flag, they will match the 52 ASCII letters and 4 additional non-ASCII letters: 'İ', 'ı', 'ſ' and 'K' (Kelvin sign). If the ASCII flag is used, only letters 'a' to 'z' and 'A' to 'Z' are matched." Contract R3 counts matches of `[a-z0-9]+` in `text.lower()` — i.e. no `IGNORECASE`, lowercase first — so plain `[a-z0-9]+` is correct as written and does not pick up those extras. Do not "helpfully" add `re.IGNORECASE` or `re.ASCII`; that would change counts and deviate from R3. — https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html#re.ASCII

13. **Nothing in the token/line pipeline is locale-dependent in Python 3, so "no locale use" (R6) is achieved by simply not calling `locale`/`setlocale`.** The remaining locale leakage points are precisely the ones covered above: stdio encoding (finding 3) and default `open()` encoding on 3.11–3.14 (finding 8), plus `os.linesep` write translation when `newline=None` (finding 2). Contract's explicit encodings/newline close all three.

## MUST-respect constraints (contract-backed; not to be deviated from)

- **M1.** Python >=3.11, standard library only; pytest for tests only; package at `wordstat/` flat layout; entry point `python -m wordstat ...` from repo root.
- **M2.** `python -m wordstat --help` exits 0 (argparse `-h` → `print_help()` on stdout, `exit(0)`).
- **M3.** argparse `prog` is exactly `wordstat` (explicit `ArgumentParser(prog="wordstat")`).
- **M4.** Read exactly one FILE, decoded as `utf-8-sig`; never read stdin; BOM excluded from `chars`.
- **M5.** Counts exactly as R3: `lines = len(text.splitlines())`, `words` = matches of `[a-z0-9]+` in `text.lower()`, `chars = len(text)`; no `re.IGNORECASE`, no locale.
- **M6.** `top` order: count descending, then word ascending; `--top` default 3; fewer than N distinct words lists all.
- **M7.** Text format is exactly four `\n`-terminated lines; with no words the last line is `top:` with **no trailing space**.
- **M8.** JSON format is exactly one line: `json.dumps(obj)` with **default separators** (`', '`, `': '`), then `\n`; key order `lines, words, chars, top`; `top` items `{"word": ..., "count": ...}` in that key order. (Do not pass `sort_keys=True` or compact separators.)
- **M9.** Output determinism (R6): stdout reconfigured to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`; no locale use; byte-for-byte identical on Windows/macOS/Linux.
- **M10.** Errors: one line to stderr, prefix `wordstat: error: `, stdout left empty; `<path>` is the FILE argument exactly as given (no normalization). Table: missing/dir/unreadable → exit 3 `<path>: cannot read file`; not valid UTF-8 → exit 3 `<path>: not valid UTF-8`; usage error (missing FILE, unknown flag, bad `--top`) → exit 2 with argparse default output whose **last stderr line** matches `^wordstat: error: `. Exit 0 on success including empty file. Exit 1 reserved for unexpected internal errors. Never a traceback.
- **M11.** `--top` must be an integer >= 1, else usage error (exit 2) — not exit 3, not a traceback.

## SHOULD recommendations

- **S1.** Call `sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")` first thing in `__main__`, before any output; optionally also `sys.stderr.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")` so error lines are also byte-stable when redirected on Windows. Per docs this is safe before any reads (R2 never reads stdin).
- **S2.** Pass `encoding="utf-8-sig"` explicitly on the input open; never rely on the default encoding (locale-dependent on 3.11–3.14 even though 3.15 defaults to UTF-8).
- **S3.** Do all parsing/validation and file reading before any stdout write, so the "stdout empty on error" invariant is structural rather than a rollback concern.
- **S4.** For `--top`, use argparse `type=int` plus a small validator that calls `parser.error(...)` (rather than `print`+`sys.exit(2)` or `SystemExit` with a custom message). That reuses argparse's `prog: error: ...` formatting and status 2, satisfying the last-line regex automatically. Keep `exit_on_error` at its default `True`.
- **S5.** Catch `OSError` (covers `FileNotFoundError`, `IsADirectoryError`, `PermissionError`) around open+read → exit 3 `cannot read file`; catch `UnicodeDecodeError` → exit 3 `not valid UTF-8`. Wrap the rest of main in a narrow guard that maps truly unexpected `Exception` to exit 1 with the same `wordstat: error: ` prefix, so no traceback ever escapes.
- **S6.** Emit the JSON object as a dict literal in the contracted key order and call `json.dumps(obj)` with no keyword arguments (default `ensure_ascii=True`, default separators, `sort_keys` default `False`) — this is the minimal form that is deterministic under the 3.7+ insertion-order guarantee.
- **S7.** When writing the four text lines, use `"\n".join(...) + "\n"` or `print(..., sep="", end="")` under the reconfigured stream; avoid `print` of multi-line strings with `end` defaulting in a way that could add an extra blank line. For the empty-`top` case, build `top:` with no trailing space (do not join an empty list and then append a separator).
- **S8.** In tests, assert exact bytes (e.g. compare `stdout.encode("utf-8")` or capture text after the same reconfigure), and cover: empty file → exit 0 with `lines: 0` / `words: 0` / `chars: 0` / `top:`; file with BOM; file with `\r\n` line endings (counts are on decoded text via `splitlines`, output still `\n`); invalid UTF-8 byte; missing file; directory as FILE; `--top 0`, `--top -1`, `--top abc`; unknown flag; missing FILE. That matrix is exactly the contract table plus R6.
- **S9.** Optional hardening: if `sys.stdout is None` (pythonw), skip or fail cleanly rather than raising `AttributeError` — documented possibility, though outside the contract's tested surface; do not let it change exit codes for the contracted paths.

With `errors="strict"` (the default), undecodable bytes raise `UnicodeDecodeError` → contract's `<path>: not valid UTF-8`. So empty file → `lines: 0`, matching contract "Exit 0 on success, including an empty file". # wordstat Feature Specification

**Status:** Not Started
**Dependencies:** None (greenfield)
**Layer:** Domain (CLI tool)
**Priority:** Critical Path
**Estimated Complexity:** ~6 tasks across 2 phases (implementation + tests)

**Authority:** `contract.md` at the repository root is the authoritative interface contract.
This specification supports it and never changes what it requires. `brief.md` is
supporting context only. Research findings are cited below; where research or common
practice would conflict with `contract.md`, the contract wins and the deviation is
recorded in section 5.6.

---

## 1. Executive Summary

`wordstat` is a small Python command-line tool that reads exactly one UTF-8 text file
and prints line, word, and character counts plus its most frequent words. It runs as
`python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE` from the repository root, uses only the
Python 3.11+ standard library (pytest for tests only), and produces byte-for-byte
deterministic output on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Errors exit with specific codes and
a single prefixed stderr line — never a traceback.

## 2. Problem Statement

### Current State

The repository contains only `brief.md`, `contract.md`, and a `.gitignore` ignoring
`__pycache__/`. There is no package, no tests, no packaging config, and no CI. The
worked example in `contract.md` was hand-verified during research: `sample.txt` yields
`lines: 3`, `words: 8`, `chars: 33`, and top-3 `cat=2 the=2 a=1` (with a trailing
newline in the file), which is consistent with R3/R4.

### Impact of Inaction

Without an explicit specification, the exact counting semantics (BOM exclusion,
no newline translation, literal `[a-z0-9]+` tokenization) and the deterministic output
contract are easy to implement subtly wrong — especially the universal-newline trap
(see finding F3) and the `Counter.most_common()` tie-order trap (F7).

## 3. Goals & Non-Goals

### Goals

- G1: Implement R1–R6 and the interface contract exactly as written in `contract.md`.
- G2: Byte-identical stdout on Windows, macOS, and Linux for identical inputs.
- G3: Clean, single-line errors with the exact exit codes 0/1/2/3 from the contract.
- G4: pytest test suite covering the contract table, both formats, and edge cases.
- G5: Runnable as `python -m wordstat ...` from the repo root with no installation.

### Non-Goals

- N1: No packaging (`pyproject.toml`, console scripts, distribution). The contract
  names only the `python -m wordstat` entry point.
- N2: No CI configuration. Cross-platform determinism is enforced by byte-exact tests
  that would pass/fail identically on any platform; the contract does not require CI.
- N3: No stdin support, no multi-file support, no recursion/globbing, no config files.
- N4: No performance work for huge files (whole file is read into memory; acceptable
  for a tiny tool).
- N5: No locale-aware or Unicode-word tokenization beyond the literal R3 rule.

## 4. Architecture

### 4.1 Package layout (flat, at repo root)

```
wordstat/
  __init__.py     # package marker (empty)
  __main__.py     # minimal: import cli.main, call it, exit with its code
  counts.py       # pure counting/formatting functions (no I/O)
  cli.py          # argparse, file reading, error mapping, output writing
tests/
  test_counts.py  # unit tests for counting and format builders
  test_cli.py     # subprocess tests for the real CLI surface
pytest.ini        # pythonpath = . so bare `pytest` imports wordstat
```

### 4.2 Data flow

1. `__main__.py` calls `cli.main()`.
2. `cli.main()` reconfigures stdout (and stderr) to UTF-8 / `\n` before any output.
3. argparse parses `[--json] [--top N] FILE` with `prog="wordstat"`.
4. The raw FILE argv string is retained for error messages (never normalized).
5. The file is read as **bytes** and decoded with `utf-8-sig` (strict). Decoding is
   the only text transform — no universal-newline translation.
6. `counts.analyze(text, top_n)` returns `{"lines", "words", "chars", "top"}`.
7. The chosen formatter renders text or JSON; the result is written to stdout once.

### 4.3 Error architecture

Parsing and reading complete before any stdout write, so "stdout empty on error" is
structural. Error mapping is explicit:

| Exception | Exit | Message body |
|---|---|---|
| `OSError` (incl. `FileNotFoundError`, `IsADirectoryError`, `PermissionError`) | 3 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
| `UnicodeDecodeError` | 3 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |
| argparse usage error | 2 | argparse default output (last stderr line `^wordstat: error: `) |
| any other `Exception` | 1 | `internal error` |

All non-argparse errors print exactly one stderr line: `wordstat: error: ` + body.
`sys.exit` is always called with an integer (never a string — `sys.exit("msg")`
exits 1 and would corrupt the exit-code contract).

## 5. Detailed Design

### 5.1 Counting (R3, R4) — pure functions in `counts.py`

```python
tokens = re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower())
lines = len(text.splitlines())
words = len(tokens)
chars = len(text)
```

- `text` is the decoded string after BOM removal; `chars` counts code points.
- Tokenization is literal `[a-z0-9]+` on `text.lower()` — no `re.IGNORECASE`, no
  `re.ASCII`, no `casefold()`, no `str.split()` (see F6, F7).
- Top ordering: `sorted(counter.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[:N]`.
  Never `Counter.most_common()` alone — its ties are first-encounter order, not word
  ascending (F7). `words` and `top` derive from the same token list (R4 "same tokens").
- `--top` default is 3; fewer than N distinct words lists all of them.

### 5.2 Output formats (R5)

**Text** — exactly four lines, each ending `\n`:

```
lines: <lines>
words: <words>
chars: <chars>
top: <word>=<count> <word>=<count> ...
```

With no words, the last line is exactly `top:` — no trailing space (build via
`"top:"` alone, not `"".join([])` plus a separator).

**JSON** — one line: `json.dumps(obj)` with **no keyword arguments** (default
separators `', '` / `': '`, `ensure_ascii=True`, `sort_keys=False`), then `\n`.
`obj` is a dict literal with keys in contract order: `lines`, `words`, `chars`, `top`,
where `top` is a list of `{"word": str, "count": int}` objects in that key order.

### 5.3 File reading (R2, R3)

- Read the path as bytes (`Path.read_bytes()` or `open(path, "rb")`), then
  `.decode("utf-8-sig")` with default `errors="strict"`.
- This guarantees: BOM excluded from `chars`; `\r` / `\r\n` preserved in the decoded
  text so `chars` counts them; a stray `U+FEFF` not at the start counts as one char.
- stdin is never read. A literal `-` FILE argument is treated as an ordinary file
  name (missing file `-` → exit 3), per decision D3.

### 5.4 Deterministic I/O (R6)

- First statement of `main()`: `sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")`.
  Also reconfigure stderr the same way (decision D4) so non-ASCII paths in error lines
  cannot raise `UnicodeEncodeError` on legacy Windows code pages.
- No `locale` module use, no `os.linesep`, no platform default encodings anywhere in
  the read/decode/output path (explicit `encoding=` on every I/O operation).
- `newline="\n"` disables `os.linesep` write translation on Windows (F2).

### 5.5 CLI (R1, contract "Command")

- `argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="wordstat")` — explicit `prog` is required because
  `python -m` would otherwise report `__main__.py` and break the `^wordstat: error: `
  last-line requirement (F5).
- `--top` uses a `type=` converter that returns `int` if `>= 1` and raises
  `argparse.ArgumentTypeError` otherwise. This makes `--top 0`, `--top -1`, and
  `--top abc` all exit 2 through argparse's own error path (decision D2).
- Keep argparse defaults otherwise (`allow_abbrev=True`, `exit_on_error=True`).
  Usage errors use "argparse default" output per the contract.
- `--help` exits 0 with help on stdout (argparse default; satisfies R1).
- `argparse.FileType` is not used (it would open stdin for `-` and leaks file handles).

### 5.6 Research decisions and rejected alternatives

Where researchers or common practice differed, `contract.md` and evidence decided:

- **D1 — Read path (analyst vs. web researchers).** The codebase analyst recommended
  `read_bytes().decode("utf-8-sig")`; the Python-API researcher offered either that or
  `open(path, encoding="utf-8-sig", newline="")`. **Decided:** bytes + decode —
  the simplest 3.11-safe form with no text-mode I/O at all. **Alternative (recorded):**
  `open(..., newline="")`, which preserves endings too but keeps a text-mode wrapper
  in the path. Rejected alternative: plain `open(...)` / `Path.read_text()` with
  default `newline=None`, which translates `\r\n`→`\n` and would undercount `chars`
  on CRLF files (F3).
- **D2 — `--top` validation.** One researcher suggested `type=int` plus a post-parse
  `parser.error(...)` check; another suggested a converter raising
  `argparse.ArgumentTypeError`. **Decided:** the converter — one code path, identical
  exit-2 message shape (`argument --top: ...`) for non-int and `< 1`. **Alternative:**
  post-parse `parser.error`, recorded and rejected as redundant.
- **D3 — literal `-` argument.** The contract says stdin is never read but does not
  name `-`. **Decided:** `-` is an ordinary FILE path (echoed exactly as given; a
  missing file named `-` exits 3). This is the option closest to "reads exactly one
  file" + "stdin is never read". **Alternatives:** reject `-` as a usage error; treat
  `-` as stdin (violates R2). Rejected.
- **D4 — stderr encoding.** The contract reconfigures stdout only. **Decided:** also
  reconfigure stderr to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"` — harmless, keeps error
  lines byte-stable and un-codable paths from crashing the error path. The stdout
  requirement remains exactly as the contract states.
- **D5 — argparse abbreviations.** **Decided:** keep `allow_abbrev=True` (default),
  because the contract defers usage-error behavior to "argparse default".
  **Alternative:** `allow_abbrev=False` for stricter "unknown flag" handling; recorded
  and rejected as a contract deviation.
- **D6 — exit-1 message.** The contract reserves exit 1 for unexpected internal errors
  but names no message. **Decided:** one stderr line `wordstat: error: internal error`,
  exit 1, no traceback (brief: "never a traceback"). **Alternative:** include the
  exception type in the message; rejected to keep output minimal and deterministic.
- **D7 — CI.** The brief requires determinism across three OSes; the contract requires
  no CI. **Decided:** no CI config (N2). Byte-exact tests enforce determinism wherever
  they run. Recorded as a trade-off in `handoff.md`.

### 5.7 Consequences to test deliberately

- `str.splitlines()` splits on `\n`, `\r`, `\r\n`, `\v`, `\f`, `\x1c`–`\x1e`, `\x85`,
  ` `, ` `; empty text → 0 lines; a terminal line break adds no extra line.
- `str.lower()` can change token boundaries for a few non-ASCII chars (e.g. `İ` →
  `i` + combining dot; `K` → `k`). Deterministic and contract-conformant; tests must
  not assume non-ASCII letters tokenize like ASCII.

## 6. Cost Estimates

Not applicable (no infrastructure or operating cost; pure local stdlib tool).

## 7. Task Outline (Preliminary)

1. **T1 — Counting core** (`wordstat/counts.py`): `analyze(text, top_n)` and format
   builders for text/JSON; pure functions only.
2. **T2 — CLI and entry point** (`wordstat/cli.py`, `wordstat/__main__.py`,
   `wordstat/__init__.py`): argparse, byte read + `utf-8-sig` decode, error mapping,
   reconfigured stdio, exit codes 0/1/2/3.
3. **T3 — Unit tests** (`tests/test_counts.py`): counting rules, ordering/ties, empty
   input, BOM/CRLF behaviors, both formatters byte-exact.
4. **T4 — CLI tests** (`tests/test_cli.py`): subprocess `python -m wordstat` matrix —
   contract example, `--json`, `--top`, `--help`, every row of the error table,
   stdout-empty-on-error, byte-exact `\n` output.
5. **T5 — Project hygiene**: `pytest.ini` with `pythonpath = .`; add `.pytest_cache/`
   to `.gitignore`; document `python -m pytest` as the test command.

## 8. Risks & Mitigations

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Universal-newline translation alters `chars` on CRLF files | Bytes-then-decode read path (F3); CRLF test case |
| `Counter.most_common()` tie order breaks R4 | Explicit `(-count, word)` sort (F7); tie test (`cat=2 the=2`) |
| Default `prog` breaks error-line regex | Hard-code `prog="wordstat"` (F5) |
| Locale-dependent default encoding on 3.11–3.14 | Explicit `encoding=` everywhere (F8) |
| `sys.exit("msg")` silently exits 1 | Integer-only `sys.exit` (F12) |
| Non-ASCII path crashes error path on Windows | Stderr reconfigure (D4) |
| Bare `pytest` cannot import `wordstat` | `pytest.ini` `pythonpath = .` |

## 9. Acceptance Criteria

Verbatim from `contract.md` (authoritative):

- AC1 (R1): `python -m wordstat --help` exits 0.
- AC2 (R2): exactly one FILE argument, UTF-8 with optional BOM (`utf-8-sig`); stdin
  never read.
- AC3 (R3): `lines = len(text.splitlines())`; `words` = matches of `[a-z0-9]+` in
  `text.lower()`; `chars = len(text)` (code points, BOM excluded).
- AC4 (R4): top-N by count desc then word asc; default N=3; fewer distinct words lists
  all.
- AC5 (R5): text format by default; `--json` selects the JSON format.
- AC6 (R6): deterministic UTF-8 `\n` output; stdout reconfigured to
  `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`; no locale use.
- AC7: text format is exactly four `\n`-terminated lines; empty-words case is `top:`
  with no trailing space.
- AC8: JSON is one `json.dumps(obj)` line (default separators) + `\n`, keys in order
  `lines, words, chars, top`.
- AC9: `--top` is an integer `>= 1`, else usage error.
- AC10: error table — missing/dir/unreadable → 3 + `<path>: cannot read file`;
  not valid UTF-8 → 3 + `<path>: not valid UTF-8`; usage error → 2 with argparse
  default whose last stderr line matches `^wordstat: error: `. All errors: one stderr
  line prefixed `wordstat: error: `, stdout empty, `<path>` echoed exactly as given.
- AC11: exit 0 on success including an empty file; exit 1 reserved for unexpected
  internal errors; never a traceback.
- AC12: the worked example in `contract.md` reproduces byte-for-byte in both formats.
- AC13: pytest suite passes via `python -m pytest` from the repo root.

## 10. Dependencies on Prior Features

None. Greenfield package.

## 11. Delegation to Future Specs

None required. Possible later work (explicitly out of scope here): CI matrix (N2),
packaging/distribution (N1), streaming for very large files (N4).

**Priority:** Critical Path
**Estimated Complexity:** ~6 tasks across 2 phases (implementation + tests)

**Authority:** `contract.md` at the repository root is the authoritative interface contract.
This specification supports it and never changes what it requires. `brief.md` is
supporting context only. Research findings are cited below; where research or common
practice would conflict with `contract.md`, the contract wins and the deviation is
recorded in section 5.6.

---

## 1. Executive Summary

`wordstat` is a small Python command-line tool that reads exactly one UTF-8 text file
and prints line, word, and character counts plus its most frequent words. It runs as
`python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE` from the repository root, uses only the
Python 3.11+ standard library (pytest for tests only), and produces byte-for-byte
deterministic output on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Errors exit with specific codes and
a single prefixed stderr line — never a traceback.

## 2. Problem Statement

### Current State

The repository contains only `brief.md`, `contract.md`, and a `.gitignore` ignoring
`__pycache__/`. There is no package, no tests, no packaging config, and no CI. The
worked example in `contract.md` was hand-verified during research: `sample.txt` yields
`lines: 3`, `words: 8`, `chars: 33`, and top-3 `cat=2 the=2 a=1` (with a trailing
newline in the file), which is consistent with R3/R4.

### Impact of Inaction

Without an explicit specification, the exact counting semantics (BOM exclusion,
no newline translation, literal `[a-z0-9]+` tokenization) and the deterministic output
contract are easy to implement subtly wrong — especially the universal-newline trap
(see finding F3) and the `Counter.most_common()` tie-order trap (F7).

## 3. Goals & Non-Goals

### Goals

- G1: Implement R1–R6 and the interface contract exactly as written in `contract.md`.
- G2: Byte-identical stdout on Windows, macOS, and Linux for identical inputs.
- G3: Clean, single-line errors with the exact exit codes 0/1/2/3 from the contract.
- G4: pytest test suite covering the contract table, both formats, and edge cases.
- G5: Runnable as `python -m wordstat ...` from the repo root with no installation.

### Non-Goals

- N1: No packaging (`pyproject.toml`, console scripts, distribution). The contract
  names only the `python -m wordstat` entry point.
- N2: No CI configuration. Cross-platform determinism is enforced by byte-exact tests
  that would pass/fail identically on any platform; the contract does not require CI.
- N3: No stdin support, no multi-file support, no recursion/globbing, no config files.
- N4: No performance work for huge files (whole file is read into memory; acceptable
  for a tiny tool).
- N5: No locale-aware or Unicode-word tokenization beyond the literal R3 rule.

## 4. Architecture

### 4.1 Package layout (flat, at repo root)

```
wordstat/
  __init__.py     # package marker (empty)
  __main__.py     # minimal: import cli.main, call it, exit with its code
  counts.py       # pure counting/formatting functions (no I/O)
  cli.py          # argparse, file reading, error mapping, output writing
tests/
  test_counts.py  # unit tests for counting and format builders
  test_cli.py     # subprocess tests for the real CLI surface
pytest.ini        # pythonpath = . so bare `pytest` imports wordstat
```

### 4.2 Data flow

1. `__main__.py` calls `cli.main()`.
2. `cli.main()` reconfigures stdout (and stderr) to UTF-8 / `\n` before any output.
3. argparse parses `[--json] [--top N] FILE` with `prog="wordstat"`.
4. The raw FILE argv string is retained for error messages (never normalized).
5. The file is read as **bytes** and decoded with `utf-8-sig` (strict). Decoding is
   the only text transform — no universal-newline translation.
6. `counts.analyze(text, top_n)` returns `{"lines", "words", "chars", "top"}`.
7. The chosen formatter renders text or JSON; the result is written to stdout once.

### 4.3 Error architecture

Parsing and reading complete before any stdout write, so "stdout empty on error" is
structural. Error mapping is explicit:

| Exception | Exit | Message body |
|---|---|---|
| `OSError` (incl. `FileNotFoundError`, `IsADirectoryError`, `PermissionError`) | 3 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
| `UnicodeDecodeError` | 3 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |
| argparse usage error | 2 | argparse default output (last stderr line `^wordstat: error: `) |
| any other `Exception` | 1 | `internal error` |

All non-argparse errors print exactly one stderr line: `wordstat: error: ` + body.
`sys.exit` is always called with an integer (never a string — `sys.exit("msg")`
exits 1 and would corrupt the exit-code contract).

## 5. Detailed Design

### 5.1 Counting (R3, R4) — pure functions in `counts.py`

```python
tokens = re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower())
lines = len(text.splitlines())
words = len(tokens)
chars = len(text)
```

- `text` is the decoded string after BOM removal; `chars` counts code points.
- Tokenization is literal `[a-z0-9]+` on `text.lower()` — no `re.IGNORECASE`, no
  `re.ASCII`, no `casefold()`, no `str.split()` (see F6, F7).
- Top ordering: `sorted(counter.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[:N]`.
  Never `Counter.most_common()` alone — its ties are first-encounter order, not word
  ascending (F7). `words` and `top` derive from the same token list (R4 "same tokens").
- `--top` default is 3; fewer than N distinct words lists all of them.

### 5.2 Output formats (R5)

**Text** — exactly four lines, each ending `\n`:

```
lines: <lines>
words: <words>
chars: <chars>
top: <word>=<count> <word>=<count> ...
```

With no words, the last line is exactly `top:` — no trailing space (build via
`"top:"` alone, not `"".join([])` plus a separator).

**JSON** — one line: `json.dumps(obj)` with **no keyword arguments** (default
separators `', '` / `': '`, `ensure_ascii=True`, `sort_keys=False`), then `\n`.
`obj` is a dict literal with keys in contract order: `lines`, `words`, `chars`, `top`,
where `top` is a list of `{"word": str, "count": int}` objects in that key order.

### 5.3 File reading (R2, R3)

- Read the path as bytes (`Path.read_bytes()` or `open(path, "rb")`), then
  `.decode("utf-8-sig")` with default `errors="strict"`.
- This guarantees: BOM excluded from `chars`; `\r` / `\r\n` preserved in the decoded
  text so `chars` counts them; a stray `U+FEFF` not at the start counts as one char.
- stdin is never read. A literal `-` FILE argument is treated as an ordinary file
  name (missing file `-` → exit 3), per decision D3.

### 5.4 Deterministic I/O (R6)

- First statement of `main()`: `sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")`.
  Also reconfigure stderr the same way (decision D4) so non-ASCII paths in error lines
  cannot raise `UnicodeEncodeError` on legacy Windows code pages.
- No `locale` module use, no `os.linesep`, no platform default encodings anywhere in
  the read/decode/output path (explicit `encoding=` on every I/O operation).
- `newline="\n"` disables `os.linesep` write translation on Windows (F2).

### 5.5 CLI (R1, contract "Command")

- `argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="wordstat")` — explicit `prog` is required because
  `python -m` would otherwise report `__main__.py` and break the `^wordstat: error: `
  last-line requirement (F5).
- `--top` uses a `type=` converter that returns `int` if `>= 1` and raises
  `argparse.ArgumentTypeError` otherwise. This makes `--top 0`, `--top -1`, and
  `--top abc` all exit 2 through argparse's own error path (decision D2).
- Keep argparse defaults otherwise (`allow_abbrev=True`, `exit_on_error=True`).
  Usage errors use "argparse default" output per the contract.
- `--help` exits 0 with help on stdout (argparse default; satisfies R1).
- `argparse.FileType` is not used (it would open stdin for `-` and leaks file handles).

### 5.6 Research decisions and rejected alternatives

Where researchers or common practice differed, `contract.md` and evidence decided:

- **D1 — Read path (analyst vs. web researchers).** The codebase analyst recommended
  `read_bytes().decode("utf-8-sig")`; the Python-API researcher offered either that or
  `open(path, encoding="utf-8-sig", newline="")`. **Decided:** bytes + decode —
  the simplest 3.11-safe form with no text-mode I/O at all. **Alternative (recorded):**
  `open(..., newline="")`, which preserves endings too but keeps a text-mode wrapper
  in the path. Rejected alternative: plain `open(...)` / `Path.read_text()` with
  default `newline=None`, which translates `\r\n`→`\n` and would undercount `chars`
  on CRLF files (F3).
- **D2 — `--top` validation.** One researcher suggested `type=int` plus a post-parse
  `parser.error(...)` check; another suggested a converter raising
  `argparse.ArgumentTypeError`. **Decided:** the converter — one code path, identical
  exit-2 message shape (`argument --top: ...`) for non-int and `< 1`. **Alternative:**
  post-parse `parser.error`, recorded and rejected as redundant.
- **D3 — literal `-` argument.** The contract says stdin is never read but does not
  name `-`. **Decided:** `-` is an ordinary FILE path (echoed exactly as given; a
  missing file named `-` exits 3). This is the option closest to "reads exactly one
  file" + "stdin is never read". **Alternatives:** reject `-` as a usage error; treat
  `-` as stdin (violates R2). Rejected.
- **D4 — stderr encoding.** The contract reconfigures stdout only. **Decided:** also
  reconfigure stderr to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"` — harmless, keeps error
  lines byte-stable and un-codable paths from crashing the error path. The stdout
  requirement remains exactly as the contract states.
- **D5 — argparse abbreviations.** **Decided:** keep `allow_abbrev=True` (default),
  because the contract defers usage-error behavior to "argparse default".
  **Alternative:** `allow_abbrev=False` for stricter "unknown flag" handling; recorded
  and rejected as a contract deviation.
- **D6 — exit-1 message.** The contract reserves exit 1 for unexpected internal errors
  but names no message. **Decided:** one stderr line `wordstat: error: internal error`,
  exit 1, no traceback (brief: "never a traceback"). **Alternative:** include the
  exception type in the message; rejected to keep output minimal and deterministic.
- **D7 — CI.** The brief requires determinism across three OSes; the contract requires
  no CI. **Decided:** no CI config (N2). Byte-exact tests enforce determinism wherever
  they run. Recorded as a trade-off in `handoff.md`.

### 5.7 Consequences to test deliberately

- `str.splitlines()` splits on `\n`, `\r`, `\r\n`, `\v`, `\f`, `\x1c`–`\x1e`, `\x85`,
  ` `, ` `; empty text → 0 lines; a terminal line break adds no extra line.
- `str.lower()` can change token boundaries for a few non-ASCII chars (e.g. `İ` →
  `i` + combining dot; `K` → `k`). Deterministic and contract-conformant; tests must
  not assume non-ASCII letters tokenize like ASCII.

## 6. Cost Estimates

Not applicable (no infrastructure or operating cost; pure local stdlib tool).

## 7. Task Outline (Preliminary)

1. **T1 — Counting core** (`wordstat/counts.py`): `analyze(text, top_n)` and format
   builders for text/JSON; pure functions only.
2. **T2 — CLI and entry point** (`wordstat/cli.py`, `wordstat/__main__.py`,
   `wordstat/__init__.py`): argparse, byte read + `utf-8-sig` decode, error mapping,
   reconfigured stdio, exit codes 0/1/2/3.
3. **T3 — Unit tests** (`tests/test_counts.py`): counting rules, ordering/ties, empty
   input, BOM/CRLF behaviors, both formatters byte-exact.
4. **T4 — CLI tests** (`tests/test_cli.py`): subprocess `python -m wordstat` matrix —
   contract example, `--json`, `--top`, `--help`, every row of the error table,
   stdout-empty-on-error, byte-exact `\n` output.
5. **T5 — Project hygiene**: `pytest.ini` with `pythonpath = .`; add `.pytest_cache/`
   to `.gitignore`; document `python -m pytest` as the test command.

## 8. Risks & Mitigations

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Universal-newline translation alters `chars` on CRLF files | Bytes-then-decode read path (F3); CRLF test case |
| `Counter.most_common()` tie order breaks R4 | Explicit `(-count, word)` sort (F7); tie test (`cat=2 the=2`) |
| Default `prog` breaks error-line regex | Hard-code `prog="wordstat"` (F5) |
| Locale-dependent default encoding on 3.11–3.14 | Explicit `encoding=` everywhere (F8) |
| `sys.exit("msg")` silently exits 1 | Integer-only `sys.exit` (F12) |
| Non-ASCII path crashes error path on Windows | Stderr reconfigure (D4) |
| Bare `pytest` cannot import `wordstat` | `pytest.ini` `pythonpath = .` |

## 9. Acceptance Criteria

Verbatim from `contract.md` (authoritative):

- AC1 (R1): `python -m wordstat --help` exits 0.
- AC2 (R2): exactly one FILE argument, UTF-8 with optional BOM (`utf-8-sig`); stdin
  never read.
- AC3 (R3): `lines = len(text.splitlines())`; `words` = matches of `[a-z0-9]+` in
  `text.lower()`; `chars = len(text)` (code points, BOM excluded).
- AC4 (R4): top-N by count desc then word asc; default N=3; fewer distinct words lists
  all.
- AC5 (R5): text format by default; `--json` selects the JSON format.
- AC6 (R6): deterministic UTF-8 `\n` output; stdout reconfigured to
  `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`; no locale use.
- AC7: text format is exactly four `\n`-terminated lines; empty-words case is `top:`
  with no trailing space.
- AC8: JSON is one `json.dumps(obj)` line (default separators) + `\n`, keys in order
  `lines, words, chars, top`.
- AC9: `--top` is an integer `>= 1`, else usage error.
- AC10: error table — missing/dir/unreadable → 3 + `<path>: cannot read file`;
  not valid UTF-8 → 3 + `<path>: not valid UTF-8`; usage error → 2 with argparse
  default whose last stderr line matches `^wordstat: error: `. All errors: one stderr
  line prefixed `wordstat: error: `, stdout empty, `<path>` echoed exactly as given.
- AC11: exit 0 on success including an empty file; exit 1 reserved for unexpected
  internal errors; never a traceback.
- AC12: the worked example in `contract.md` reproduces byte-for-byte in both formats.
- AC13: pytest suite passes via `python -m pytest` from the repo root.

## 10. Dependencies on Prior Features

None. Greenfield package.

## 11. Delegation to Future Specs

None required. Possible later work (explicitly out of scope here): CI matrix (N2),
packaging/distribution (N1), streaming for very large files (N4).
